source_refs.note: Topic 19.4.2 with the For Information and Analyse and Interpret boxes, answered (PDF 132). The book's degeneracy example is corrected in a note.

items: Universal: the code is the same in almost all organisms (AGA specifies arginine in bacteria, humans and all others), which is why genes can be transferred between organisms. There are a few exceptions: the mitochondrial code differs slightly, reflecting the separate evolutionary history of mitochondria, and some organisms such as ciliates and some viruses such as bacteriophages use different codes.
Triplet: the code is in three-nucleotide codons, which balances the information in DNA with that needed for 20 kinds of amino acid.

Degenerate: more than one codon can specify the same amino acid. For example, four different codons (AUG, GUG, UUG and CUG) code for the same amino acid, methionine. This helps tolerate mutations and gives evolutionary flexibility.
Without punctuation: codons are read continuously, with no gaps between them.
Non-overlapping: each triplet is read independently of its neighbours, so AUGAGCGCA is read only as AUG/AGC/GCA, never as AUG/UGA/GAG.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's example of degeneracy, AUG, GUG, UUG and CUG all coding for methionine, is wrong: only AUG codes for methionine; GUG codes for valine, and UUG and CUG for leucine (they can act as start codons in some bacteria). A correct example: four different codons, GUU, GUC, GUA and GUG, code for the same amino acid, valine.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: The exceptions to the universal code show that, although the standard code is widely used, there is still room for variation and adaptation in it.
